name: aji
title: aji
definition: Aji — literally "taste" — in weiqi is latent potential: the residual possibilities in dead or weak stones, or in a defect in the opponent's shape, that are not currently playable but that constrain what both sides can do. The standard maxim is that aji is used by not using it — a threat that has already been played is no longer a threat.

name: aji-keshi
title: aji-keshi
definition: Aji-keshi ("erasing the aji") in weiqi is playing a move that forces the opponent to answer in a way that removes the player's own latent options — the residual aji a position was carrying. It is one of the most characteristic strong-player errors: the move usually gains something locally, but it spends a possibility that was worth more unspent.

name: area-scoring
title: area-scoring
definition: Area scoring in weiqi computes each player's final score as the number of that player's own live stones remaining on the board plus the vacant points that count as that player's territory; captures made during play matter only insofar as they change which stones are on the board at the end, not as separately counted prisoner points. Chinese, New Zealand, and Ing rules all use area scoring. Because a stone on the board and an enclosed empty point are worth the same one point each, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs nothing under area scoring: it simply converts a territory point into a stone point.

name: atari
title: atari
definition: Atari in weiqi is the state in which a stone or connected group has only one liberty remaining and is therefore under immediate threat of capture.

name: capture
title: capture
definition: A capture in weiqi occurs when a move removes the last liberty from an opposing stone or connected group, after which those stones are removed from the board.

name: connection
title: connection
definition: A connection in weiqi is a relation between stones that makes them function as one group, sharing liberties and supporting each other's defense.

name: dame
title: dame
definition: Dame in weiqi are the neutral, empty points left on the board that border stones of both colors and belong to neither player's territory.

name: dango
title: dango
definition: Dango ("dumpling") in weiqi is a clump of stones bunched together with few liberties relative to their number, an overconcentrated shape that gains little board coverage for the stones spent on it. A dumpling shape is inefficient specifically because it duplicates work: several stones end up defending the same small set of liberties that fewer, better-placed stones would have secured.

name: dead-stones
title: dead-stones
definition: Dead stones in weiqi are stones left on the board after both players pass that cannot avoid eventual capture under correct play, and are therefore removed as though captured before the board is counted, without either player having to actually play out the capture. A stone or group is dead exactly when it fails the same test life-and-death reading always applies: it cannot make two secure eyes and cannot escape or be rescued. A group that shares unresolvable liberties with the opponent, by contrast, is in seki and is never marked dead.

name: eye
title: eye
definition: An eye in weiqi is an empty point or enclosed space inside a group's shape that functions as an internal liberty and helps determine whether the group can live.

name: false-eye
title: false-eye
definition: A false eye in weiqi is an eye-shaped empty point that looks like a protected internal liberty but does not meet the diagonal-control and connection requirements of a real eye, so the opponent can eventually force the surrounding group to fill it.

name: fuseki
title: fuseki
definition: Fuseki in weiqi is the opening considered as a whole board, as distinct from joseki, the memorized locally-balanced corner sequences a fuseki is built from. Where a joseki is judged by whether it is locally balanced, a fuseki is judged by whether the whole-board framework it builds serves the position — a joseki that is correct in isolation can still be the wrong choice for the fuseki around it.

name: geta
title: geta
definition: Geta ("net") in weiqi is a technique for capturing a stone or small group by surrounding it loosely, from a distance, with a small number of stones placed so that any attempt to extend toward a liberty runs into a stone already in place. The captured stones are never chased liberty by liberty; the net is set once, and the group inside it cannot escape by any single move.

name: gote
title: gote
definition: Gote in weiqi is a move that ends the mover's turn because the opponent need not answer it. It is the complement of sente: where a sente sequence lets its player keep the initiative and play elsewhere next, a gote sequence hands the initiative to the opponent.

name: handicap
title: handicap
definition: A handicap in weiqi is a rule adjustment, usually extra Black stones placed before play begins, that lets players of unequal strength compete in a meaningful game.

name: honte
title: honte
definition: Honte in weiqi is the solid, "proper" move — the one that leaves no aji behind, at the cost of a little tempo. Kageyama's Lessons in the Fundamentals of Go is the standard source on honte, alongside shape and direction of play, and the concept exists specifically to name the trade a greedier, more aji-leaving move refuses to make.

name: hoshi
title: hoshi
definition: Hoshi in weiqi are the nine marked star points on a 19x19 board, used as fixed handicap-stone locations and as visual landmarks for opening play, with the center star point known as tengen. The nine points sit at the 4-4 point in each corner, the 4-10 point on the midpoint of each edge, and the 10-10 point at the exact center of the board.

name: influence
title: influence
definition: Influence (seiryoku) in weiqi is the effect a stone or group exerts on the space around it without enclosing it. It is not territory-in-waiting, and treating it as such is the classical beginner error: influence's value is that it constrains the opponent's options, making invasions in its neighbourhood expensive or unlivable, so the opponent must play elsewhere while the influence-holder collects the difference.

name: joseki
title: joseki
definition: Joseki in weiqi are the memorized, locally-balanced corner sequences catalogued across the standard literature, most exhaustively by Ishida's three-volume Dictionary of Basic Joseki. Each joseki is a locally complete exchange in which neither side gains a clear local advantage; the players agree, in effect, to a fair local trade and both move on.

name: keima
title: keima
definition: Keima ("knight's move") in weiqi is playing a stone one point away from an existing stone in one direction and two points away in the perpendicular direction, the same offset a knight moves on a chessboard. Like tobi, it is not a physical connection; it covers ground faster than a solid connection at the cost of a gap the opponent can, in principle, exploit.

name: kikashi
title: kikashi
definition: Kikashi in weiqi is a forcing move played for the value of the response it compels rather than for the stone's own local worth, kept as a quick exchange rather than developed further. The player spends one move, the opponent must answer it in a fixed way, and the player keeps sente to play elsewhere — the exchange is judged complete the moment it is made.

name: ko
title: ko
definition: Ko in weiqi is a repetition constraint that forbids a player from making the immediate recapture that would recreate the previous board position.

name: komi
title: komi
definition: Komi in weiqi is the point compensation added to White's final score to offset Black's first-move advantage.

name: liberty
title: liberty
definition: A liberty in weiqi is an empty intersection directly adjacent to a stone or connected group of stones. Liberties determine whether a group remains on the board. When the last liberty is removed, the group is subject to capture.

name: life-and-death
title: life-and-death
definition: Life and death in weiqi is the analysis of whether a group can secure enough stable shape, usually through eyes, to avoid capture, or whether the opponent can force it off the board.

name: miai
title: miai
definition: Miai in weiqi are two points of equal value such that, if the opponent takes one, the player takes the other. Miai converts a contested point into a settled one: once two points are miai, a player can safely ignore both, playing elsewhere, and answer only after the opponent commits to one.

name: moyo
title: moyo
definition: Moyo in weiqi is a large-scale framework of potential territory, outlined by stones' influence rather than enclosed by them. A moyo is influence organized at whole-board scale and aimed at a specific outcome — growing into secured space — where bare influence only constrains the opponent's options without claiming any of them.

name: pass
title: pass
definition: A pass in weiqi is a legal turn in which a player declines to place a stone, leaving the board unchanged and giving the move to the opponent. Passing is always available; it is never restricted by ko, suicide, or any other placement rule, since it places nothing. Two consecutive passes, one by each player in immediate succession, end the main phase of play and open dead-stones settlement and scoring; if the players cannot agree during that settlement, play conventionally resumes from the pass to resolve the disagreement by capture.

name: sabaki
title: sabaki
definition: Sabaki in weiqi is making a light, flexible, quickly-settled shape inside the opponent's sphere of influence, playing so that any individual stone is expendable. It contrasts with heavy (omoi) shape, which must be saved at all costs and therefore becomes a target the opponent can attack repeatedly for profit.

name: seki
title: seki
definition: Seki in weiqi is a standoff in which two or more groups of opposite color share their remaining liberties, and neither side can play into the shared liberties without reducing its own group to a liberty count the opponent can then capture on the next move. Neither group has two eyes, yet neither can be captured either, so both remain on the board unresolved for the rest of the game. Seki is a genuine third outcome for a local fight, distinct from either group living outright or dying.

name: semeai
title: semeai
definition: Semeai ("capturing race") in weiqi is a contest between two adjacent groups, neither of which has secured two eyes, where each side fills the other's liberties as fast as possible and the group that runs out first is captured. It differs from an ordinary atari chase because both groups are mutually vulnerable at once — the racing side must count whether it can fill the opponent's last liberty before its own runs out, not merely whether it can force the opponent into atari.

name: sente
title: sente
definition: Sente in weiqi is the initiative: a move the opponent must answer, so that the player who made it may play again elsewhere. Gote is its complement, a move that ends the mover's turn because the opponent need not answer. A sequence is sente for a player if that player retains the initiative through it.

name: suicide
title: suicide
definition: Suicide in weiqi is a move that would leave the moving player's own stone or group with zero liberties after any opposing stones it removes are taken off the board. Under most rulesets suicide is simply illegal: a player may not place a stone that reduces their own group to no liberties unless that same move first captures an opposing group and thereby restores at least one liberty. New Zealand rules are the well-known exception, permitting suicide of any size — a player may play a stone, or fill their own group's last liberties entirely, and the played stones are then immediately removed as self-captured.

name: superko
title: superko
definition: Superko in weiqi is a repetition rule that extends ko beyond the single immediately-preceding position: it forbids recreating any whole-board position that has already occurred in the game, not only the one position just before the opponent's last move. Two variants are in common use. Positional superko (PSK) forbids any recurrence of an identical arrangement of stones, regardless of whose turn it is. Situational superko (SSK) forbids a recurrence only when it is also the same player's turn to move as it was the earlier time that arrangement occurred — so the same stone arrangement may legally recur once with the other player to move, but not a second time with the original player to move.

name: sute-ishi
title: sute-ishi
definition: Sute-ishi ("throw-away stones") in weiqi are one or more stones deliberately played to be captured, because the exchange the capture forces is worth more than the stones would have been worth kept alive. The player plans the loss before the opponent takes it; the stones are bait, not a mistake later rationalized as sacrifice.

name: territory
title: territory
definition: Territory in weiqi is the set of vacant points effectively enclosed by one player's stones and unavailable to the opponent except at unacceptable cost.

name: territory-scoring
title: territory-scoring
definition: Territory scoring in weiqi computes each player's final score as the vacant points that count as that player's territory plus the prisoners that player captured from the opponent during the game; a live stone remaining on the board at the end contributes no direct point value of its own. Japanese and Korean rules use territory scoring. Because stones themselves are not counted, playing an extra move inside your own territory late in the game costs a full point under territory scoring: it removes one territory point and, since nothing was captured, adds nothing back.

name: thickness
title: thickness
definition: Thickness (atsumi) in weiqi is a strong, settled, outward-facing formation with no weakness the opponent can exploit locally. Three classical maxims describe what thickness is not: do not use it to enclose territory, since walling off space wastes the wall's real value; do not play close to thickness, yours or the opponent's, since stones near a thick wall are cheap for its owner to attack; and thickness is a property of the position, not of the stones, so the same wall is strong against an empty board and worthless once the opponent has a living group settled behind it.

name: tobi
title: tobi
definition: Tobi ("jump") in weiqi is playing a stone one empty point away from an existing stone along a line, leaving the intersection between them unoccupied. A two-space jump extends the same idea one point further; both are not physically connected the way an adjacent stone is, but are functionally connected in most fighting situations because the opponent cutting at the gap usually costs more than it gains.

name: zenkyoku
title: zenkyoku
definition: Zenkyoku ("whole board") in weiqi is evaluating a move by its effect on the balance of the entire board rather than judging the local exchange in isolation. A move read as locally correct can still be the wrong move once its effect on a distant, seemingly unrelated group is counted; zenkyoku is the discipline of checking that effect before playing.
